State any three postulates of Dalton's atomic theory.
questions.a: Matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; atoms combine in small whole-number ratios to form compounds.

questions.q: Which part of Dalton's theory was proved wrong?
questions.a: Atoms are divisible (into subatomic particles), and atoms of one element can differ slightly in mass (isotopes).

questions.q: How does Dalton's theory explain the laws of chemical combination?
questions.a: Atoms rearrange without change in number or mass (conservation of mass) and combine in fixed ratios (constant proportions).

questions.q: What is a covalent bond?
questions.a: A bond formed by sharing of electron pairs between two atoms, as in H2, O2 or CH4.

questions.q: Why do atoms share electrons instead of transferring them?
questions.a: Sharing lets both atoms complete their outermost shell without the large energy cost of full transfer.

questions.q: How many electrons are shared in a double bond? Give an example.
questions.a: Two pairs (4 electrons), as between the two oxygen atoms of O2.

questions.q: What is an ionic bond?
questions.a: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electrons, as in NaCl.

questions.q: How does magnesium oxide form ionically?
questions.a: Magnesium loses 2 electrons to oxygen; Mg2+ and O2- attract each other strongly to form MgO.

questions.q: Why are ionic compounds brittle?
questions.a: On striking, like-charged ions come face to face and repel, so the crystal breaks.

questions.q: State the rules for writing the formula of an ionic compound.
questions.a: Write the symbols with charges, cross over the charges as subscripts, and simplify to the simplest whole-number ratio.

questions.q: How is the formula of aluminium sulphate written?
questions.a: Al3+ and SO4 2- cross over to give Al2(SO4)3.

questions.q: Why are charges not shown in the final formula?
questions.a: The compound is neutral overall; the crossed subscripts already balance the charges.

concepts.title: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds

questions.q: Compare melting points of ionic and covalent compounds.
questions.a: Ionic compounds melt at high temperatures because strong ion-ion forces must be broken; many covalent compounds melt easily.

questions.q: Which conducts electricity - molten NaCl or liquid hexane? Why?
questions.a: Molten NaCl - its free ions move and carry current; hexane has no charged particles.

questions.q: Name two properties of covalent compounds.
questions.a: Poor conductors, low melting/boiling points, usually insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
